extracted.intended_audience: researchers, institutional press officers/PIOs, journal editors and science communicators
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and accountability criteria for academic (especially health) press releases—what they must include, avoid, and how institutions/authors should behave to prevent exaggeration and misleading coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author attribution / named authors
rubrics_metrics.description: Author(s) named (not anonymous PIO); authors should be publicly named and linked to the press release.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Press releases should include the actual researchers' names (not only institutional press office). Author attribution supports reputation accountability and ties claims to identifiable responsible parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Link to original paper
rubrics_metrics.description: Press releases should be linked to original peer-reviewed paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always provide a direct link to the underlying article so journalists and readers can check the source, methods and limitations themselves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public posting of press releases
rubrics_metrics.description: Press releases should be posted publicly (not just sent to media).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make releases permanently available on institutional websites to enable public scrutiny, citation, and tracking of later exaggeration or corrections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match strength of source paper claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Press release claims should match the strength of the source paper claims (no overstatement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid amplifying tentative or limited findings into stronger claims than supported by the study design or evidence; framing should reflect level of certainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish causal versus correlational findings
rubrics_metrics.description: Causal language must not be used for correlational studies; causal vs correlational distinguished.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly state when associations do not imply causation; avoid wording that implies causation unless the study design and analysis justify it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish animal/cell research from human research
rubrics_metrics.description: Generalizing animal/cell research to humans should be avoided; press releases must distinguish animal/cell vs human findings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make clear whether results were observed in animals, cells, or humans and avoid implying direct human relevance when only preclinical work exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include study limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Limitations included; press releases must be assessable for limitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State key weaknesses, uncertainty, and boundaries of inference so users can judge applicability; do not suppress limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclose conflicts of interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Conflicts of interest disclosed; press releases should not suppress conflicts of interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List relevant COIs transparently (authors' financial ties, commercial involvement) to allow independent assessment of potential bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclose funding sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Funding sources disclosed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify funders and any funder role in study design, analysis, or the press release itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report absolute effect sizes
rubrics_metrics.description: Effect sizes reported in absolute terms (not only relative measures).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer absolute risks or differences so readers grasp real-world magnitude rather than misleading-sounding relative percentages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include confidence intervals / uncertainty estimates
rubrics_metrics.description: Confidence intervals included; quantify uncertainty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide CIs or other appropriate statistical uncertainty measures rather than relying solely on point estimates or p-values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid 'breakthrough' or 'cure' language without basis
rubrics_metrics.description: No 'breakthrough' without basis; no 'cure' language without basis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use hype words (e.g., 'breakthrough', 'cure') unless the evidence unequivocally supports such claims; sensational terms should be justified or omitted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish hypothetical from observed findings
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguishes hypothetical from observed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit when discussing hypothetical mechanisms, modelling, or speculations versus directly observed empirical results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Researcher review and approval
rubrics_metrics.description: Researchers should review press releases before issue; authors should sign off on claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institute a requirement that authors review and approve any press material about their work to ensure accuracy and agreement on claim strength.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communicate data accurately
rubrics_metrics.description: Press releases should communicate data accurately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accuracy applies to results, methods description, and stated implications; avoid cherry-picking or selective emphasis that distorts the study's message.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow free and open access to release content
rubrics_metrics.description: Allow free and open access.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make press releases and linked materials openly accessible so journalists and the public can read them without barriers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be intelligible to specialists
rubrics_metrics.description: Be intelligible to specialists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While aimed at media/public, releases should still be clear and precise enough for other specialists to assess the study's design and findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be assessable and usable by other specialists
rubrics_metrics.description: Be assessable for limitations and usable by other specialists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include sufficient methodological detail or links to enable specialist readers to evaluate and, if relevant, reproduce or build upon the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid giving implicit advice not in the paper
rubrics_metrics.description: Implicit advice not in paper should be avoided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not insert policy, clinical, or behavioral advice beyond what the study directly supports; separate speculation/advice from evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Track exaggeration and media pickup over time
rubrics_metrics.description: Track exaggeration patterns / track media coverage for exaggeration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monitor how press releases are reported and whether claims are subsequently exaggerated; use tracking to evaluate institutional practices and identify problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publish corrections when needed
rubrics_metrics.description: Publish corrections when needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When errors or exaggerations are identified in releases or their media coverage, issue transparent corrections and link them to the original release.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use peer-review-style approval before issuing releases
rubrics_metrics.description: Use peer-review-style approval before issue (institutional implementation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt internal review processes—possibly modeled on peer review—to check accuracy and appropriateness of claims prior to dissemination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain accountability dashboards / public accountability mechanisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain accountability dashboards; use public shame as an accountability tool.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create visible metrics and public records of press release quality and corrections to encourage institutional improvements and reputational incentives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post releases on institutional sites with author attribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Post press releases on institutional sites with author attribution (modern implementation practice).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Centralized posting enables discoverability, archiving, and linking between releases and original research; include named authors and links to the paper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reputation accountability for authors
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors held accountable by reputation for the content of releases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Naming authors and requiring sign-off creates reputational incentives for accuracy; institutions should emphasize this responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence that accurate/cautious releases do not reduce coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Accuracy and cautious framing do not reduce media pickup (Sumner finding).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use evidence (e.g., Sumner et al.) to counter concerns that accurate or cautious press releases will lead to less media attention—accurate sources may gain long-term credibility and coverage.
